ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Chi-square(3)=8.74 gives p≈.033 not .003 — requires mental computation or lookup
ground_truth.original_snippet: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.033.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003.
ground_truth.description: Changed p from .033 to .003 — chi-square(3)=8.74 yields p~.033 not .003; makes marginal finding appear robust

matched_finding.description: Sadness omnibus p-value appears incorrect: The omnibus p-value for sad words appears to be incorrect. A $\chi^2$ statistic of 8.74 with 3 degrees of freedom corresponds to about $p=.033$, which is also the value reported in Table 2, not $p=.003$. The Results text reports the same statistic as $p=.003$, so the text likely overstates the strength of this result.
matched_finding.quote:
Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, $2(3)=8.74$, $\mathrm{p}=.003$. Pairwise
comparisons revealed that attempt episodes were significantly higher in sad words compared to ideation ( $\mathrm{z}=2.64$, $\mathrm{p}=.008$ ), but not compared to depressed or positive $\operatorname{mood}(\mathrm{zs}=1.07-1.09, \mathrm{ps}=.277-.285)$.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Typical vs positive mood changes comparison gradient — must understand risk-level anchoring
ground_truth.original_snippet: two-week episode of positive mood (i.e., more positive mood than usual and no ideation or attempt).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt).
ground_truth.description: Changed positive mood to typical/neutral mood — compresses risk gradient, eliminates theoretical contrast between suicidal states and genuinely positive states

matched_finding.subcategory: Low-risk episode label shifts from typical to positive
matched_finding.description: Low-risk episode label shifts from typical to positive: The operationalization of the lowest-risk comparison condition is ambiguous: the interview list defines the fourth category as typical mood, “neither particularly positive nor negative,” while other sections label this category positive mood or positive episodes. Since positive emotion and emotional tone are outcomes, it should be clear whether participants identified neutral/typical periods or positively valenced periods. This distinction affects interpretation of the risk gradient and comparisons involving the “positive” episode type.
matched_finding.quote:
Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a "suicide attempt episode"; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt). (Note that reported 'suicide attempts' also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than 'suicide ideation' so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.) The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort to capture the critical period of increased ideation, planning, and intent leading up to a suicide attempt (Millner et al., 2016). The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced. Specifically, temporal visualizations, using a smoother (loess) function, were constructed for each variable of interest and consisted of graphs plotting daily means for the given variable during the 30 days prior to and following the attempt. Although highly variable across variables, changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt. A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events. For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes (e.g., three suicide attempts if participant has three or more lifetime attempts). Millner et al., 2016Millner et al., 2016

Critically, classifications of these reported episodes became the basis of the study's within-subjects design, with episode type serving as our main predictor variable and language characteristics of text messages during the episodes as the outcome variables. In terms of suicide risk levels, attempt episodes were considered "high risk," ideation episodes were considered "moderate risk," and depressed and positive episodes were considered "minimal/no risk."

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Self-focus vs rumination — must know these are distinct constructs in suicidology

ground_truth.modified_snippet: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts
ground_truth.description: Changed 'self-focus' to 'rumination' — different constructs (Baumeister escape theory vs Nolen-Hoeksema response styles); first-person pronouns index self-referential attention, not repetitive negative thinking

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Means show increase (0.82→1.03) but text says 'decreased' — arithmetic contradiction
ground_truth.original_snippet: and desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: and desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.
ground_truth.description: Changed post desire-to-die from 0.61 to 1.03 — means now show INCREASE while text says 'decreased'; safety-critical inconsistency in iatrogenic check

matched_finding.description: Misreported direction of iatrogenic effects: The iatrogenic-effects result appears to reverse the direction of the desire-to-die change: the reported means go from pre $M=0.82$ to post $M=1.03$, and Table 1 reports a positive pre-to-post change for desire to die, yet the text says desire to die 'significantly decreased slightly.' Unless the scale was reverse-scored, this should be treated as a significant increase and the safety interpretation adjusted accordingly. The sentence cannot describe the result as a slight decrease unless the means, scoring, or verbal interpretation are corrected.
matched_finding.quote: However, as a precautionary measure, participants were asked two questions regarding negative mood and desire to die both at the beginning and at the conclusion of the lab session to assess any changes as a consequence of the interview and study visit.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Creates internal contradiction detectable within the paper
ground_truth.original_snippet: using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”
ground_truth.modified_snippet: using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”
ground_truth.description: Changed 'two-week' to 'one-week' in episode definition but all other references say 'two weeks' / '14 days' — cross-section inconsistency

matched_finding.subcategory: Inconsistent attempt episode window across sections
matched_finding.description: Inconsistent attempt episode window across sections: The attempt-window definition is internally inconsistent: the Procedure paragraph describes dates of attempts whereas the comparison states are two-week episodes, the interview section refers to a one-week pre-attempt episode, and the analysis plan later models days -14 to 0. Additionally, the Abstract and the Overview and Hypotheses section describe the acute-risk window as the two weeks preceding a suicide attempt. The methods should make clear which pre-attempt window actually entered the SMS analyses and how it was made comparable with the other episode types.
matched_finding.quote: Participants were invited into the laboratory for one 2 - to 2.5 -hour session to complete several tasks. First, participants were instructed to download their private data sources (e.g., SMS). Second, participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes, including dates of past suicide attempts (and interrupted or aborted attempts) and two-week episodes of suicide ideation, depressive mood, and positive mood. Participants were then asked to describe specific details of and context surrounding each time period. Last, participants completed the aforementioned questionnaires.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the Charlottesville community.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Social support vs social engagement — subtle construct distinction
ground_truth.original_snippet: In theory, social support should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: In theory, social engagement should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: No random slopes with marginal p-values — must know Barr et al recommendations
ground_truth.original_snippet: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.
ground_truth.description: Removed all random slopes (kept only intercepts) — fails to account for participant variability in episode effects; inflates Type I error per Barr et al (2013); key p-values near .05 may become false positives

matched_finding.subcategory: Omission of random slopes contradicts claims and inflates Type I error
matched_finding.description: Omission of random slopes contradicts claims and inflates Type I error: The final Primary Analysis 2 model appears to omit all random slopes after the maximal model failed to converge. Because episode type, day, and their interaction are within-participant predictors, a random-intercepts-only structure may make the fixed-effect interaction tests anti-conservative if slopes vary across participants. The Limitations section should also be reconciled with this methods statement, because it later describes the models as using maximal or near-maximal random effects. The random-effects description appears overgeneralized, and the fitted structure for the temporal slope analyses should be distinguished from the mean-difference models. The Type I error-control rationale invoked does not apply uniformly to the paper's main temporal interaction tests. Furthermore, the limitation about an “elaborate” random-effects structure appears to overgeneralize across the model families, as it is unclear whether the claimed power/generalizability tradeoff applies to the key slope results or mainly to the mean-difference analyses. Finally, the multiplicity caveat should be qualified because random intercepts address clustering but are not a maximal or near-maximal random-effects structure for the within-subject episode type by time effects.
matched_finding.quote: The maximal random effects model appropriate for these data included random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes for episode type, day of episode, and episode type by day. Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Claims all 27 had attempt data but only 15 did — must check if 27=27 makes sense given design
ground_truth.original_snippet: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt.
ground_truth.description: Concealed that only 15/27 (56%) had attempt SMS data — hides selection bias in who contributes to the critical attempt vs non-attempt comparisons

matched_finding.subcategory: Inconsistent reporting of the number of attempt episodes
matched_finding.description: Inconsistent reporting of the number of attempt episodes: The number of suicide-attempt episodes with usable SMS data is unclear. The statement that all 27 participants with SMS data had data from at least one reported suicide attempt seems to imply at least 27 attempt episodes, whereas the next subsection refers to 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data and the power section refers to 20 usable SMS attempts. These quantities may reflect different denominators, but the distinctions need to be explicit because they determine the sample size for the high-risk condition.
matched_finding.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, $134(46 \%)$ episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants. Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt.
